reviewSession.heading: Classifying information and assets: objective 2.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 2 together, one objective at a time, starting with classification. Classification sorts things by the harm that exposure, change or loss would cause, so that the cost of protection matches the value. The order to remember is management support and policy, find what you have, name an owner, classify, protect, then train and review. The owner chooses the class, and technical staff carry it out. People mix up the word Confidential, because it is the lowest secret government level and often the highest company level. They also forget that an asset takes the class of the most sensitive item on it. Government levels from the top are Top Secret, Secret, Confidential, Unclassified. When an answer offers to buy a tool before you know what you hold, it is usually wrong.

reviewSession.heading: Handling rules: objective 2.2
reviewSession.body: Now for handling. Rules are written per class, and they cover marking, storage, use, transport and disposal. The protection follows the information into every copy and every format, so a backup needs the same care as the original. Marking is for people to read, and a label is for machines. Mark public items too, so that a missing mark stands out, and treat anything unmarked as the highest class until the owner confirms it. In transport, encrypt, seal, and keep a chain of custody, which is a signed record of who held the item. Keep the class off the outer wrapping of highly sensitive items. Keep keys apart from the data. The favorite trap is lowering a class to meet a deadline. Only the owner may change a class, and convenience is never the reason.

reviewSession.heading: Provisioning, ownership and inventory: objective 2.3
reviewSession.body: Next comes secure provisioning. Give people only what the job needs. Need to know decides which information they may see, and least privilege decides what they may do with it. The owner approves, the technical team carries out, and the rights come back when the job changes. Owners can delegate the work, but they keep the accountability. An asset with no owner is an asset nobody protects, so have management name one. The inventory must hold tangible assets, which you can touch, and intangible ones, such as data, licenses and patents. People forget the intangible half, and it is often worth the most. When a discovery scan disagrees with the list, investigate first. And if an audit finds things missing, choose the answer that fixes the process, not the answer that buys replacements.

reviewSession.heading: The six data roles: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: This is the most tested part of the domain, so let us be exact. The owner is a senior manager who is accountable, sets the class and decides on access. The custodian, usually technical staff, carries out the daily care, such as backups. The user follows the rules. Those three are found inside the organization. The controller decides why and how personal data is used. The processor is a separate party that follows the controller's instructions. The subject is the living person the data is about. People wrongly call an internal technical team a processor, when it is a custodian. A processor that decides purposes for itself is treated as a controller for that use. Hiring a processor never ends the controller's accountability. If a question asks who decides, look for the owner or the controller.

reviewSession.heading: Lifecycle, collection, location and maintenance: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: Let us review the lifecycle. The six stages are create or collect, store, use, share, archive and destroy, and the class travels with the data throughout. On collection, gather only what you need for a stated purpose, tell people why, have a lawful basis, and do not quietly reuse data for something new. The best control for unneeded data is not to have it, so be wary of answers that encrypt what should never have been collected. On location, data sovereignty is about whose law applies, and data residency is about where data must sit. Check backups as well as the main copy, and check the law and contracts before moving anything. Encryption does not cancel those rules. On maintenance, keep data accurate, review access, patch systems, recheck the class, and test your restores.

reviewSession.heading: Retention and product age: objectives 2.4 and 2.5
reviewSession.body: Now retention. Keep data as long as law, contract and business need require, and no longer. Destroying too early and keeping too long can both break the law. A legal hold overrides normal deletion until it is lifted, even when the written policy says to delete. On product age, end of life means the maker stops making or selling the product. End of support means the maker stops giving updates, so no more security fixes will come. End of support is the more dangerous date, and replacement should be planned and budgeted before it. If an old system has to stay, the best answer combines isolation or other compensating controls with formal risk acceptance by management. Do not choose an answer that keeps it running because it has always been stable, or one that shuts the business down.

reviewSession.heading: Remanence and the three sanitization levels: objective 2.4
reviewSession.body: Let us go over removing data. Data remanence is what is left behind after an attempt to remove it. Deleting and normal formatting usually remove only the pointers, so neither one is sanitization. The three levels, from weakest to strongest, are clear, purge and destroy. Clearing defeats normal software tools, and it suits reuse inside the organization at the same class. Purging makes recovery infeasible even in a laboratory, and it suits media leaving your control. Destroying also leaves the media unusable, and it suits the most sensitive data. People assume that a purge always ruins a device, but a secure-erase command leaves the drive working. To choose, ask how sensitive the data is, whether the media will leave your control, and what type of media it is. Then verify the result and keep a record.

reviewSession.heading: Degaussing, crypto-erase and solid-state drives
reviewSession.body: These two methods have limits that the exam loves. Degaussing uses a strong magnetic field, and it works only on magnetic media, such as hard disk drives and tapes. It does nothing to solid-state drives, which store data on chips, or to optical discs. A stronger machine does not change that. It also usually ruins a hard drive, so it cannot be the answer when the drive must keep working. Solid-state drives move data around and keep spare areas, so overwriting can miss copies. Use the maker's secure-erase function, crypto-erase, or physical destruction. Crypto-erase means destroying the keys, and it needs strong encryption from the start and the removal of every copy of the key, including any in a recovery safe. It is the natural answer for cloud storage, where you cannot touch the disks.

reviewSession.heading: Data states, scoping and tailoring: objective 2.6
reviewSession.body: Now objective 2.6. Data is at rest when stored, in transit when moving across a network, and in use when in memory or on a screen. Data in use is the hardest to protect, and disk or network encryption does nothing for a record on a visible screen. A baseline is a starting list of minimum controls. Scoping removes the controls that do not apply. Tailoring adjusts what is left to fit. So scoping cuts and tailoring fits, and the exam will try to swap them. In United States government guidance, tailoring is the wider word that includes scoping. Keep a written reason and management approval for each change, and remember that a legal duty cannot be scoped out. When choosing standards, law comes first, then contract, then voluntary good practice. Payment card rules usually bind you through contracts, not law.

reviewSession.heading: Choosing between DRM, DLP and CASB: objective 2.6
reviewSession.body: Let us finish the tools. Digital Rights Management, or DRM, follows the file, and controls what someone can do after receiving it. Data Loss Prevention, or DLP, guards the exits, and looks for sensitive data trying to leave. It can run on the network, on staff computers or in storage, and encrypted traffic can hide data from it. A Cloud Access Security Broker, or CASB, sits between users and cloud services, shows what is being used, and applies rules. So read the need closely. If a partner already has the file, choose DRM. If something must not leave, choose DLP. If the concern is unapproved or uncontrolled cloud use, choose CASB. Remember too that masking hides, tokenization swaps data for a stand-in, and pseudonymized data is still personal data, because it can be linked back.

reviewSession.heading: How to choose the best answer in this domain
reviewSession.body: Here is how to think when a Domain 2 question looks hard. First, ask who should decide. Very often the right answer is the owner, and the tempting answer is a capable technical person. Second, ask what comes first. Knowing what you have comes before buying tools, and checking the law comes before moving data. Third, look for the cause. If a process is failing, fix the process and do not just treat the single event. Fourth, match the protection to the value, so be cautious of answers that protect everything the same way. Fifth, check the media type before choosing a sanitization method. And finally, think like a manager and adviser. People's safety comes first, then follow policy and the law, and make sure that the right person has made and recorded the decision.
